name: Escin

card.summary: The main saponin mixture of horse chestnut (Aesculus hippocastanum), used for its vascular and anti-swelling properties and in cosmetic formulas aimed at puffiness.
card.note: Best-studied for chronic venous insufficiency; puffy-skin use is based on the same swelling-related mechanisms.

quick.overview:
Escin (aescin) is a mixture of saponins from horse chestnut seeds, and its beta-escin form is the main active component. It is described as having anti-inflammatory, vasoconstrictive and vessel-protecting effects.

For appearance, it appears in depuffing formulas on the reasoning that swelling and fluid retention show up as puffiness around the eyes and legs. Clinical research is mainly on chronic venous insufficiency, where horse chestnut seed extract has been compared with compression stockings.
quick.how: Escin is used as an oral horse chestnut seed extract or as a topical ingredient in gels and creams. Cosmetic users apply it in eye and leg products.
quick.risks: Raw horse chestnut seed is toxic, and regulated extracts are standardised for this reason. Side effects reported with extracts include stomach upset and itching. People on anticoagulants or with kidney or liver disease are usually advised to consult a clinician.

lead: Escin, also spelled aescin, is a mixture of saponins from the horse chestnut Aesculus hippocastanum and accounts for most of the plant's medicinal activity; the main compound is beta-aescin [1]. It is described as anti-inflammatory, vasoconstrictive and vasoprotective [1].

Its link to looks is reduced swelling and puffiness. Horse chestnut extract is used in cosmetics for under-eye and leg puffiness; the supporting science concerns oedema and venous function more broadly. A Cochrane review of horse chestnut seed extract for chronic venous insufficiency is cited by Wikipedia, and its authors call for more high-quality randomised trials [1].
Other research includes a trial comparing aescin with diclofenac for swelling after wisdom-tooth surgery and studies of its pharmacokinetics [2][3].

chain: Escin affects vessel permeability and tone
Less fluid leakage and swelling in tissue
angle.text: Escin is used in depuffing products because it acts on venous tone and swelling. Users apply it to puffy eyes or legs hoping to lessen visible swelling.

paras: Escin is used in cosmetic formulas for puffiness, building on its vasoprotective and anti-swelling properties [1].

Wikipedia notes evidence that pure beta-aescin is safe and effective for short-term treatment of chronic venous insufficiency, and that horse chestnut extract may work about as well as compression stockings [1].

Proposed mechanisms include increased endothelial nitric oxide synthesis through greater calcium permeability, release of prostaglandin F2-alpha, antagonism of serotonin and histamine, and reduced breakdown of tissue mucopolysaccharides [1]. A 2025 review covers anti-inflammatory effects of saponins from herbs [4].
A 1996 randomised crossover study examined beta-escin pharmacokinetics after different Aesculus extract formulations [5].

A randomised double-blind trial compared aescin with diclofenac sodium for swelling and inflammation markers after impacted lower third-molar surgery [2]. Another randomised study compared aescin with prednisolone in ureteral stones [6].

Human studies of escin cover chronic venous insufficiency, post-surgical swelling and other conditions [1][2][6]. No published trial found here tests escin specifically for facial or under-eye puffiness.
